```{r}
library(tidyverse)

library(mice)
library(skimr)
library(ggplot2)
```


```{r}
#| warning: false
#| message: false

theme_ceor <-theme_bw() +
  # theme(legend.position = "none")+
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(size = 24,hjust=-0.03),
    axis.line = element_line(colour = "black"),
    panel.grid.major = element_blank(),
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
    panel.border = element_blank(),
    panel.background = element_blank(),
    axis.text=element_text(size=16),
    axis.title=element_text(size=18),
    axis.line.x = element_line(size = 0.5, linetype = "solid", colour = "black"),
    axis.line.y = element_line(size = 0.5, linetype = "solid", colour = "black")
  )

```


The simple or easy way to deal with incomplete data is just remove it. However, this could let to the reduction of a big portition of the data and when the data is difficult to obtain or the fact that are missing could shown a hidden pattern. For those reasons we need to extract the best with the data we have.

The objective of this notebook is to implement the examples in the book @b_2012_vanBuuren_FlexibleImputationOfMissingData_Chapman.

There are different types of missing data and here is a nomenclature of the types of missing data we can encounter:

* **MCAR** : Missing Completely At Random.
* **MAR** : Missing At Random.
* **MNAR** : Missing Not At Random.



## Simple Data Analysis

Following the book @b_2012_vanBuuren_FlexibleImputationOfMissingData_Chapman we use a dataset shipped by default with R `airquality`.

I particularly prefer to use tibbles instead of a classic data.frame in R

```{r}
df_airquality <- airquality %>% tibble()
```


and a simple inspection of the data can be done with the glimpse command and

```{r}
glimpse(df_airquality)
```

However, we could use the DT package to present all (or part) of the data in interactive datatable 

```{r}
DT::datatable(df_airquality, filter="top")
```

To get what is distribution and order or magnitude of quantities in the table we can get a summary of the data 


```{r}
summary(airquality)
```


Notice that there are a couple of columns in `airquality` dataset (Ozone and Solar.R) that have with NA values. More especifically Ozone has 37 NA and Solar.R 7 and we can get a better representation of this summary usig gtsummary package @tbl-airquality-summary:

```{r}
#| label: tbl-airquality-summary
#| tbl-cap: Table for automatic reports using gtsummary tbl_summary

gtsummary::tbl_summary(df_airquality)
```


### Simple linear regression


```{r}
model1  <- lm(Ozone ~ Solar.R + Wind, data=airquality)
model1 %>% gtsummary::tbl_regression()
```


```{r}
ic(airquality) %>% head(5)
```

```{r}
pred <- predict(model1, newdata=ic(df_airquality) %>% head(5))
pred
```


```{r}
df_trial <- gtsummary::trial
df_trial %>% gtsummary::tbl_summary()
```

```{r}
summary(df_trial)
```

```{r}
df_trial
```

```{r}
plt_tmp <- airquality %>% 
ggplot() +
geom_point(aes(x=Solar.R, y=Ozone, color=Wind)) +
labs(x="Solar.R", y="Ozone")+
theme_ceor
```
